n: The Preacher looks at oppression and sees the tears of victims with no one to comfort them, while their oppressors hold all the power. The repeated phrase stresses their loneliness.
Overwhelmed by such suffering, he says the dead seem better off than the living who must endure it.
Better still, he says, is the one never born, who never had to see the evil done on earth. This is honest lament, not a teaching that life lacks worth.
Much hard work and success is driven by envy and rivalry with one’s neighbor. Competition of that kind is just chasing the wind.
On the other hand, the lazy fool who folds his hands ends up destroying himself. Idleness is no answer either.

f.g: Ruins himself; starves by his own laziness.

n: The balanced path: one handful with peace is better than two handfuls gained through stress and striving.
He turns to another example of life’s emptiness.
A man with no family works endlessly and is never satisfied with his wealth. He never stops to ask who he is working for or why he denies himself joy.
Companionship makes work more rewarding. Two people working together accomplish more than one alone.
If one falls, the other can help him up. The person who has no one is in real danger when trouble comes.

f.w: woe to him that is alone

n: On cold desert nights, travelers slept close for warmth. Companions protect and comfort one another.
Two can defend against an attacker better than one, and a rope of three strands is very hard to break. Many readers see in this a picture of marriage with God as the third strand.

f.g: A rope braided from three strands — far stronger than one or two.

n: A poor young person who is wise is better than an old king who will no longer listen to advice. Position means nothing without teachableness.
Such a youth may rise from prison to the throne, while one born royal may end up poor. Fortunes can reverse completely.

f.w: out of prison he cometh to reign
f.g: Recalls Joseph rising from prison to rule in Egypt (Genesis 41:14, 41).

n: He watches crowds rally behind the young successor who replaces the old king.

f.g: The youth who succeeds the king.

n: Yet the crowds are endless, and the next generation will forget even the popular new leader. Public favor is fleeting too.
